newsitem.title: USA: World Bank sees first debt relief pacts by yearend.
newsitem.headline: World Bank sees first debt relief pacts by yearend.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn said on Friday the international community was near agreement on a debt relief plan for poor countries and expected the first cases to be dealt with by yearend.
"My guess is that between now and the end of the year we will have our first cases," Wolfensohn said.
"I think we're very close to reaching a positive and productive agreement that will allow us to proceed immediately on specific cases," he said.
Wolfensohn conceded that details remain to be worked out, noting that the Paris Club of creditor nations had yet to announce the specifics of their part of the debt relief plan.
The International Monetary Fund and World Bank have called for the Paris Club to forgive some 90 percent of loans but Wolfensohn said it would be less than that, though he was uncertain by how much.
"I don't know if it's 80 percent but it certainly not going to be 90 percent," he said.
Oxfam International, a private development group, lashed out at the apparent decision to reduce the forgiveness to less that 90 percent.
"Without a clear commitment from the Paris Club to reduce 90 percent of debt, the viability of the entire initiative could be undermined," the group said in a statement.
Diplomatic sources said there appears to be consensus emerging in the Paris Club to offer debt relief of up to 80 percent on a case-by-case basis.
It currently provides relief of up to 67 percent under so-called Naples terms.
Wolfensohn met with reporters ahead of the annual meetings of the Bank and International Monetary Fund at which the debt plan is a key agenda item.
The aim is to provide debt relief not just from creditor nations but also from the IMF and World Bank, whose loans to poor countries have themselves become a problem.
The Paris Club has long said it is willing to improve debt relief to very poor countries provided the IMF and World Bank themselves do their own share in helping them.

The plan has generated considerable controversy because the IMF had recommended the sale of a small portion of its gold hoard to help fund its programme as well as finance its existing Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility.

But IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus made clear on Thursday that while the programme was a "done deal," the gold sales would only be considered if funding by donor countries, the World Bank and the Fund itself fell short.
In his remarks, Wolfensohn said the Bank had already committed some $500 million to the effort and he was prepared to recommend that a total $2 billion be pledged in the years ahead.

Leaders of the Group of Seven rich nations agreed at a summit in Lyon, France, last June that debt relief should be improved for the world's poorest nations, with the Paris Club, IMF and World Bank all playing a role.
G7 finance ministers from the United States, Germany, France, Britain, Italy, Canada and Japan were expected to discuss the debt plan when they meet on Saturday.
